citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): "A dynamic hip screw... allows for compression at the fracture site on load-bearing and protects the femoral head from penetration by the screw when the osteoporotic bone settles."

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: In which specific portion of the distal femur are osteoporotic fractures most likely to occur?
back: The metaphyseal region.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 437 (Book Page): "Metaphyseal osteoporotic fractures of the distal femur are amenable to internal fxation..."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: A fracture that occurs when abnormal bone fails under a normal physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the primary pathophysiological difference between traumatic and pathological fractures?
back: Traumatic: Excessive force on healthy bone. Pathological: Physiological (normal) force on weakened/diseased bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture. ... The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast clinical history findings in traumatic vs. pathological fractures.
back: Traumatic: Consistent with high-energy force. Pathological: History is inconsistent with the severity of the injury (e.g., low-energy fall causing major fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A patient sustains a femur fracture while simply walking across a room. What is the suspected diagnosis?
back: Pathological fracture, likely secondary to an underlying condition weakening the bone as it failed under normal weight-bearing load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Which haematological malignancies are known to cause pathological fractures?
back:
● Myeloma
● Lymphoma
● Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What metabolic bone diseases serve as common underlying causes for pathological fractures?
back:
● Osteomalacia
● Paget’s disease
● Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis)]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why are 'load-bearing' implants prioritized over 'load-sharing' devices in pathological fractures?
back: Abnormal bone involved in pathological fractures may fail to heal, necessitating an implant that can support the entire load independently.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Differentiate the radiological management of impending vs. actual pathological fractures in metastatic disease.
back: If a metastatic deposit is identified before failure, 'prophylactic stabilization' with a load-bearing device is advocated to prevent fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the defining feature of a 'compound' or 'open' fracture regardless of being pathological or traumatic?
back: The fracture haematoma communicates with a breach in an epithelial lining (skin, mucosa, vagina, or rectum).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [an open fracture being any fracture where the fracture haematoma communicates with a breach in the epithelial lining, not just skin.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What non-malignant infectious process can lead to bone weakening and pathological fracture?
back: Osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by ... osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: A fracture occurring when abnormal bone fails under a normal, low-energy load that would not typically cause injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why do pathological fractures require load-bearing rather than load-sharing implants?
back: The underlying diseased bone often has poor healing potential and cannot be relied upon to support structural loads.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Differentiate pathological from traumatic fractures based on the energy of injury.
back:
● Pathological: Low-energy/trivial force (e.g., normal walking).
● Traumatic: High-energy force (e.g., RTA, fall from height) on normal bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture... In contrast, traumatic fractures involve normal bone failing under excessive load.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A patient sustains a femur fracture after a simple trip. What is the clinical priority?
back: The clinician must suspect a pathological cause and actively investigate for underlying malignancy or metabolic bone disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List the metabolic bone diseases associated with pathological fractures.
back:
● Osteomalacia
● Paget’s disease
● Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the clinical hallmark for suspecting a pathological fracture during history taking?
back: A history of injury that is inconsistent with the actual clinical severity or degree of displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the surgical management strategy for an impending pathological fracture?
back: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing device to prevent the fracture from occurring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered... Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the management of isolated versus multiple metastatic pathological fractures.
back:
● Isolated (Curative): En bloc excision.
● Multiple (Palliative): Stabilization with a load-bearing device to maintain function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device... If an isolated metastasis is identifed... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How do haematological malignancies cause pathological fractures?
back: Systemic cancers like myeloma, lymphoma, and leukaemia weaken the internal bone structure, allowing failure under normal physiological loads.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What defines the primary bone failure in osteoporotic pathological fractures?
back: Low bone mineral density and significantly reduced structural strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporosis is a condition characterised by low bone mineral density and reduced strength. Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What are the two defining pathological characteristics of osteoporosis?
back:
1. Low bone mineral density (BMD).
2. Reduced bone strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): Osteoporosis is a condition characterised by low bone mineral density and reduced strength.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
coreConcept: Disuse Osteoporosis in Spinal Cord Injury
front: Q: Which specific trauma-related condition results in inevitable disuse osteoporosis?
back: Spinal cord injury, due to the loss of physiological load and movement on the skeleton.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence of spinal cord injury and fragility fractures may occur.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which patient demographic is at the highest risk for thoracic wedge compression fractures?
back: Older adults (typically associated with osteoporosis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What degree of force is sufficient to cause a fracture in osteoporotic bone?
back: Low-energy force, such as a fall from standing height.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which specific medication class should be screened in an MSK history as a risk factor for bone loss?
back: Steroids (Corticosteroids).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 493 (Book Page): Check about all medication and the following in particular:... steroids.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
coreConcept: Age and Gender as Risk Factors
front: Q: Beyond age, which gender is specifically identified as having negatively impacted bone healing and quality?
back: Female gender.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 436 (Book Page): increasing age and female gender further negatively impact on fracture healing.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: A patient with spinal cord injury develops a femur fracture from a minor turn in bed. Explain the pathology.
back: Fragility fracture occurring as a result of established disuse osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence of spinal cord injury and fragility fractures may occur.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which metabolic disease should be considered during MSK evaluation as a risk for secondary hyperparathyroidism?
back: Renal disease (End-stage renal failure).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): Renal disease... Secondary hyperparathyroidism may be present.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What specific anatomical risk complicates the surgical fixation of osteoporotic fractures?
back: Soft bone in the metaphysis, which causes rigid fixation devices to 'cut out'.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 432 (Book Page): rigid fxation devices may cut out of soft bone, particularly in the metaphysis of the bone where pull-out strength of the fxation is reduced.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
coreConcept: Hormonal Risk Factors for Bone Density
front: Q: What historical female health factors should be queried regarding bone health risk?
back:
1. Use of oral contraceptive pill.
2. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 493 (Book Page): oral contraceptive pill and hormone replacement therapy.

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Which specific spinal segment is most commonly affected by osteoporotic wedge compression fractures?
back: Thoracic spine (T1–T10).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group. ... (T1–T10)]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Define the typical injury mechanism for fractures in osteoporotic bone.
back: Low-energy trauma, such as a fall from standing height.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Identify the two primary lower limb sites for osteoporotic fractures.
back: 1. Proximal femur (Hip); 2. Distal femur (Metaphysis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [lower limb osteoporotic fractures in older patients ... metaphyseal osteoporotic fractures of the distal femur.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
coreConcept: Clinical identification of osteoporotic hip fracture
front: Q: Scenario: An elderly patient falls. Examination shows a shortened, externally rotated leg. Identify the fracture site.
back: Proximal femur (Hip).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [A shortened externally rotated leg in an older patient suggests a fracture of the proximal femur.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Which pharmacological class reduces fracture rates by decreasing bone resorption and turnover?
back: Bisphosphonates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Identify the primary radiographic criterion for diagnosing an osteoporotic vertebral fracture.
back: Wedge compression morphology (loss of anterior vertebral body height).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Why is the metaphysis a high-risk site for osteoporotic fracture fixation failure?
back: Reduced bone mineral density leads to decreased screw pull-out strength in the metaphyseal region.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 432 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic intra-articular fractures ... particularly in the metaphysis of the bone where pull-out strength of the fxation is reduced.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Identify common upper limb periarticular sites for osteoporotic fractures requiring replacement.
back: 1. Proximal humerus (Shoulder); 2. Radial head (Elbow).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 436 (Book Page): [older patients with osteoporotic periarticular fractures ... shoulder hemiarthroplasty, radial head replacement.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Describe the Hueter-Volkmann principle as it relates to skeletal remodelling after fracture.
back: Compressive forces inhibit bone growth, while tensile forces stimulate growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
front: Q: Identify the most common osteoporotic fracture site in the wrist.
back: Distal radius (Colles’ fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Most dorsally displaced fractures (Colles fracture) can be addressed...]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: A fracture occurring when abnormal bone fails under a normal load that would not typically break healthy bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the primary clinical difference in the history of a pathological versus traumatic fracture?
back:
● Pathological: Low-energy injury inconsistent with injury severity.
● Traumatic: High-energy force consistent with injury severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the healing potential of pathological and traumatic fractures.
back: Traumatic fractures usually heal; pathological fractures may never heal depending on the underlying etiology (e.g., malignancy or radiotherapy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How does surgical implant choice differ for pathological fractures likely to fail healing?
back: Surgeons prioritize "load-bearing" devices over "load-sharing" devices because the weak bone cannot be relied upon to eventually carry weight.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List three haematological malignancies that commonly cause pathological fractures.
back:
1. Myeloma
2. Lymphoma
3. Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What metabolic bone diseases are risk factors for pathological fractures?
back:
● Osteoporosis
● Osteomalacia
● Paget’s disease
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the management priority if a fracture is suspected to be due to a primary bone tumour?
back: Treatment must be planned to prevent disseminating the disease (e.g., staging and controlled biopsy before fixation).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A patient with an identified metastasis has an impending fracture. What is the surgical priority?
back: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing device to prevent the fracture and preserve mobility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: In which pathological fracture scenario is en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty preferred?
back: In isolated secondary metastatic deposits with a good oncological prognosis or for primary curative intent near a joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why is Paget’s disease classified as a cause of pathological rather than traumatic fractures?
back: It involves metabolic disruption of normal bone homeostasis, weakening the internal architecture to fail under physiological stress.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: According to the text, what are the two primary skeletal characteristics of osteoporosis?
back: 1. Low bone mineral density. 2. Reduced bone strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporosis is a condition characterised by low bone mineral density and reduced strength.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: How does spinal cord injury physiologically serve as a risk factor for bone loss?
back: It leads to disuse osteoporosis due to the lack of physiological loading and mechanical stress on the skeleton.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence of spinal cord injury and fragility fractures may occur.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Distinguish between the fracture liability of normal bone versus osteoporotic bone regarding injury energy.
back: Normal bone resists standing-height falls; osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g., minor slips).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: A 22-year-old female athlete presents with amenorrhoea and a stress fracture. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back: Female athlete triad, consisting of: 1. Osteoporosis. 2. Disordered eating. 3. Amenorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 628 (Book Page): [female athlete triad (osteoporosis, disordered eating and amenorrhoea)]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What metabolic step do bisphosphonates target to improve strength in density-deficient bone?
back: They decrease bone resorption and turnover, which reduces fracture rates and promotes weight-bearing mobility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What anatomical finding is diagnostic of osteoporosis in the thoracic spine of elderly patients?
back: Wedge compression fractures (commonly found at levels T1 to T10).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Apply Wolff’s Law to explain why immobile patients develop osteoporosis.
back: Since bone resorption depends on applied stresses, reduced physiological loading leads to increased resorption and density loss.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [Wolff’s law: Bone deposition and resorption depend on the stresses applied.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Why are low-energy injuries in older patients a critical indicator of osteoporosis?
back: They indicate reduced bone strength where fractures occur from forces that uninjured bone would normally tolerate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: How does disordered eating specifically contribute as an osteoporosis risk factor in athletes?
back: It functions as a metabolic trigger within the female athlete triad, directly leading to early-onset bone density loss.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 628 (Book Page): [Stress fractures are also found in female dancers as a result of repetitive training and can be more frequent in the female athlete triad (osteoporosis, disordered eating and amenorrhoea)]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which specific age demographic is most frequently associated with osteoporotic thoracic spinal injuries?
back: Older adults (the elderly).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture in skeletal clinical practice.
back: - A fracture that occurs when abnormal or diseased bone fails under a normal or low-energy load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Explain the mechanical rationale for using load-bearing implants in pathological fractures.
back:
- Pathological bone often fails to heal reliably.
- Load-bearing devices provide permanent structural support independent of the bone's biological union.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast traumatic and pathological fractures regarding the energy of the injury mechanism.
back:
- Traumatic: High-energy force applied to normal bone.
- Pathological: Low-energy force (which normally would not cause injury) applied to weakened bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: An elderly patient fractures a femur after simply rolling in bed. Classify this injury pattern.
back:
- Pathological Fracture.
- Justification: The history of minor movement is inconsistent with the severity of a femoral fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List three common metabolic bone diseases that cause pathological fractures.
back:
- Osteomalacia
- Paget’s disease
- Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the primary clinical hallmark used to differentiate pathological from traumatic fractures during history taking?
back: - Mechanism inconsistency: The severity of the bone failure does not match the minor force of the reported trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: When is prophylactic surgical fixation indicated for a patient with metastatic bone disease?
back: - When a metastatic deposit is identified on imaging and a fracture is clinically impending.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Differentiate the surgical handling of periarticular metastases versus primary bone tumors.
back:
- Metastases: Often treated with en bloc excision and immediate joint arthroplasty to optimize early function.
- Primary Tumors: Planned carefully to prevent disease dissemination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If the deposit is periarticular, an en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty may be considered... Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Explain why bone stabilization is prioritized even in palliative cases of pathological fractures.
back:
- To allow early full weight-bearing.
- To bypass the need for biological healing in diseased bone.
- To restore patient mobility and quality of life.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Arthroplasty in suitable patients bypasses the problems of blood supply and weak bone and allows early full weight-bearing and return to function.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List three common non-metabolic sources of underlying bone weakness leading to pathological fractures.
back:
- Primary bone tumors
- Secondary metastatic deposits
- Osteomyelitis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits... osteomyelitis]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the formal definition of a pathological fracture?
back: A fracture that occurs when abnormal bone fails under a normal, physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How do pathological fractures primarily differ from traumatic fractures regarding injury mechanism?
back: Pathological fractures occur following low-energy trauma inconsistent with injury severity, whereas traumatic fractures occur when excessive force is applied to normal bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the healing potential of pathological fractures versus standard traumatic fractures.
back: Traumatic fractures usually heal predictably; pathological fractures (especially due to malignancy) may not heal, requiring specialized load-bearing fixation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: An elderly patient sustains a femur fracture after a simple standing trip. What must be ruled out?
back: Pathological fracture. The low-energy mechanism is inconsistent with the severity of the bone failure, necessitating a search for underlying systemic disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture. If a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List the metabolic bone diseases that commonly cause pathological fractures.
back:
● Osteomalacia
● Paget’s disease
● Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Which haematological malignancies are known to weaken bone and cause pathological fractures?
back:
● Myeloma
● Lymphoma
● Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Differentiate the surgical implant requirements for pathological vs. traumatic fractures.
back: Pathological fractures require load-bearing implants (which assume the entire load) rather than load-sharing implants because the bone may never unite.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Pathological fractures may not heal and require load-bearing not load-sharing implants]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How is an impending pathological fracture managed differently from a traumatic one?
back: Traumatic fractures are managed post-injury; impending pathological fractures are managed preemptively with prophylactic stabilization using load-bearing devices.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Name the primary infective cause of pathological fractures.
back: Osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by ... osteomyelitis]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the first clinical clue that a fracture is pathological?
back: A history of trauma that is significantly too mild to have caused the resulting bone failure in healthy individuals.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture in musculoskeletal medicine.
back: A fracture occurring when abnormal bone fails under a level of load that would normally be considered physiological or non-traumatic.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the mechanical differentiation between pathological and traumatic fractures?
back: Traumatic fractures involve high-energy forces applied to healthy bone. Pathological fractures involve normal physiological forces applied to bone weakened by pre-existing disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture. If a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the surgical implant choice for pathological versus traumatic fractures.
back: Pathological fractures often require load-bearing devices (e.g., intramedullary nails) rather than load-sharing ones, as the underlying bone quality may not heal or provide support.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A 65-year-old female presents with a femur fracture after a simple trip. What is the primary clinical suspicion?
back: Suspect a pathological fracture due to the inconsistency between the low-energy mechanism and the resulting skeletal failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Which three categories of metabolic bone disease commonly cause pathological fractures?
back:
1. Osteomalacia
2. Paget’s disease
3. Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What are the three defining hematological malignancies that result in weakened bone and pathological fractures?
back:
1. Myeloma
2. Lymphoma
3. Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the indicated management for an impending pathological fracture in a patient with known metastatic disease?
back: Prophylactic stabilisation using a load-bearing device is recommended to prevent displacement and improve outcomes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Differentiate the surgical approach for a non-reconstructible articular pathological fracture versus a simple articular traumatic fracture.
back: Articular traumatic fractures are reduced and fixed. Pathological fractures that are non-reconstructible may require en bloc excision and primary joint replacement (arthroplasty).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What physiological cycle is disrupted in pathological fractures caused by infection?
back: Bacterial invasion (osteomyelitis) leads to local inflammatory responses and abscess formation, which increases intraosseous pressure, disrupts blood supply, and destroys bone architecture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis... If a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List the four primary malignant categories (excluding primary tumors) that predispose to pathological fractures.
back:
1. Secondary metastatic deposits
2. Myeloma
3. Lymphoma
4. Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)...]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which demographic is at the highest risk for osteoporotic wedge compression fractures?
back: Older adults (incidence increases with age due to declining bone mineral density).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Why is spinal cord injury identified as a significant risk factor for osteoporosis?
back: It results in disuse osteoporosis, which is an inevitable consequence of prolonged immobilisation and lack of mechanical loading.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence of spinal cord injury and fragility fractures may occur.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Contrast the primary nutritional and malabsorptive risk factors for bone mineralisation failure.
back:
1. Nutritional: Reduced Vitamin D and Calcium intake.
2. Malabsorptive: Crohn's disease and gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Nutritional: Reduced intake of vitamin D and calcium... Gastrointestinal disease: Crohn’s disease, gluten-sensitive enteropathy]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: A 75-year-old female sustains a hip fracture from a standing-height fall. What is the suspected underlying risk factor?
back: Osteoporosis (indicated by susceptibility to fragility fractures from low-energy mechanisms).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which pharmacological agent is a major risk factor for secondary bone fragility and poor healing?
back: Corticosteroids (chronic steroid use).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [address medical conditions that may impair wound healing (e.g. smoking, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, steroid use) prior to surgery.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What are the two defining clinical characteristics of the condition of osteoporosis?
back:
1. Low bone mineral density.
2. Reduced bone strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporosis is a condition characterised by low bone mineral density and reduced strength.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: How do diabetes and smoking serve as risk factors for osteoporotic bone complications?
back: They impair tissue perfusion and biological healing, increasing the risk of fracture non-union and poor bone turnover.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Well-known factors that slow down bone healing include diabetes mellitus... smoking...]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Differentiate an osteoporotic fracture from one caused by a primary bone tumour.
back:
1. Osteoporotic: Systemic failure due to metabolic bone disease.
2. Primary Tumour: Localised bone weakening (pathological fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: How does end-stage renal failure contribute as a metabolic risk factor for bone disease?
back: It causes secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal tubular anomalies, leading to inadequate bone mineralisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Renal disease: End-stage renal failure, renal tubular anomalies. Secondary hyperparathyroidism may be present]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What environmental factor is a primary risk factor for Vitamin D-related bone mineralisation failure?
back: Inadequate exposure to sunlight.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Environmental: Inadequate exposure to sunlight]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: A fracture occurring through abnormal bone failing under normal load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the injury force of traumatic versus pathological fractures.
back:
● Traumatic: High-energy force matches injury severity.
● Pathological: Low-energy force inconsistent with injury severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List three haematological malignancies that cause pathological fractures.
back:
1. Myeloma
2. Lymphoma
3. Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Which metabolic bone diseases predispose to pathological fractures?
back:
● Osteomalacia
● Paget’s disease
● Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A patient with known breast cancer suffers a humerus fracture after merely reaching for a cup. Diagnosis?
back: Pathological fracture secondary to metastatic bone disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury... secondary metastatic deposits]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why is internal fixation preferred over casting for lower limb osteoporotic fractures in the elderly?
back: To allow immediate weight-bearing and early mobilization, as these patients often have pre-existing mobility problems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [As there may be additional and pre-existing mobility problems, such patients are unable to partially weight-bear and so fixation should be strong enough to allow immediate weight-bearing]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the implant choice for pathological versus normal fractures.
back:
● Pathological: Load-bearing devices (implants carry all weight).
● Normal: Load-sharing devices (bone helps carry weight).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the primary management goal for a solitary metastasis with good prognosis?
back: Aggressive curative approach with en bloc excision of both primary and secondary deposits.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identified and an overall good prognosis is offered... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How does chronic osteomyelitis cause a pathological fracture?
back: Bone destruction and abscess formation lead to structural weakness and avascularity, predisposing it to failure under load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page)/635: [The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis... the pressure effects secondary to the abscess formation lead to bony destruction.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define prophylactic fixation in the context of metastatic bone disease.
back: Stabilization of the bone with a load-bearing device before an impending fracture actually occurs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identified prior to fracture, prophylactic fixation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilization with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: A fracture occurring when abnormal or weakened bone fails under normal physiological load or trivial trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the primary mechanical difference between traumatic and pathological fractures?
back:
Traumatic: High-energy force on normal bone.
Pathological: Low-energy/trivial force on weakened bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How does the surgical stabilization principle differ for pathological versus traumatic fractures?
back:
Pathological: Prefers load-bearing implants (bone may never heal).
Traumatic: Prefers load-sharing implants (bone is expected to heal).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A patient presents with a fracture from a minor slip; what specific clinical feature suggests it is pathological?
back: History is inconsistent with injury severity (low-energy mechanism that usually would not cause a fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List four systemic malignancies that commonly cause pathological fractures.
back:
1. Secondary metastatic deposits
2. Myeloma
3. Lymphoma
4. Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Name three non-malignant conditions that weaken bone and cause pathological fractures.
back:
1. Osteomyelitis
2. Paget’s disease
3. Osteomalacia/Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the mandatory first step when a pathological fracture from a suspected primary bone tumor is identified?
back: Careful treatment planning to prevent disseminating the disease (biopsy and staging).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the surgical approach for isolated versus multiple secondary metastatic bone deposits.
back:
Isolated: Aggressive curative en bloc excision.
Multiple: Palliative stabilization with load-bearing devices.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered. If an isolated metastasis is identifed... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why is arthroplasty often preferred over internal fixation for elderly patients with pathological periarticular fractures?
back: It bypasses risks of non-union and poor blood supply, allowing immediate full weight-bearing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Arthroplasty in suitable patients bypasses the problems of blood supply and weak bone and allows early full weight-bearing and return to function.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What defines an 'impending' pathological fracture?
back: A metastatic deposit identified prior to structural failure where fracture is considered likely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely.]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture according to clinical standards.
back: A: A fracture that occurs when abnormal bone fails under a normal physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the load requirements in traumatic vs. pathological fractures.
back:
• Traumatic: Abnormal/excessive load applied to healthy bone.
• Pathological: Normal/physiological load applied to diseased bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture. [Context: Traumatic fractures involve abnormal forces].

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: What is the primary clinical indicator that a fracture is pathological rather than traumatic?
back: A: A history where the mechanism of injury (low-energy) is inconsistent with the resulting fracture severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How should an identified 'impending' pathological fracture be managed surgically?
back: A: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing device (rather than load-sharing).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Which pharmacological agent is used to reduce the fracture rate in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: A: Cyclical bisphosphonates (reduces bone resorption and increases mineral density).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment... reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List four common metabolic and infectious causes of pathological fractures.
back:
1. Osteoporosis
2. Osteomalacia
3. Paget’s disease
4. Osteomyelitis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why are load-bearing implants preferred for pathological fractures compared to traumatic ones?
back: A: Diseased bone in pathological fractures often fails to unite, requiring the implant to support the load permanently.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: A patient with multiple bone lesions presents after a minor trip. What must be ruled out?
back: A: Pathological fracture through a metastatic deposit or haematological malignancy site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): In patients with metastatic bone disease... A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Describe the metabolic loop leading to pathological fractures in Paget's disease.
back: A: Disordered bone remodeling results in architecturally weak bone that fails under normal stress.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Which haematological malignancies are associated with pathological fractures?
back:
• Myeloma
• Lymphoma
• Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): The bone may be weakened by... haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia).

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What defines the primary clinical characteristic of osteoporosis according to the text?
back:
- Low bone mineral density.
- Reduced bone strength.
- Increased liability to fractures from low-energy trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporosis is a condition characterised by low bone mineral density and reduced strength. Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Why is spinal cord injury identified as a significant risk factor for osteoporosis?
back:
- It results in disuse osteoporosis.
- It is considered an inevitable consequence of the injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence of spinal cord injury and fragility fractures may occur.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Contrast the bone mineralisation defect in rickets versus the pathology of Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back:
- Rickets: Inadequate mineralisation of the bone matrix.
- OI: Qualitative or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page)-615: [In rickets, the primary problem is inadequate mineralisation of growing bone... Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What patient-specific factor hinders the operative management of osteoporotic fractures in the elderly?
back:
- Presence of pre-existing mobility problems.
- Inability to tolerate partial weight-bearing protocols postoperatively.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [As there may be additional and pre-existing mobility problems, such as patients are unable to partially weight-bear and so fxation should be strong enough to allow immediate weight-bearing]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: How do bisphosphonates stabilize bone in patients with severe metabolic density loss?
back:
- Decreases bone resorption.
- Decreases bone turnover.
- Increases overall bone strength and reduces fracture rates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: Which specific fracture pattern is the most common spinal complication of osteoporosis in older adults?
back:
- Wedge compression fractures.
- Occurs most frequently in the thoracic spine.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: List three secondary nutritional and environmental risk factors for inadequate bone mineralisation.
back:
- Reduced intake of Vitamin D and Calcium.
- Inadequate sunlight exposure.
- Gastrointestinal disease (e.g., Crohn’s).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Table 44.5 Common causes of rickets... Nutritional: Reduced intake of vitamin D and calcium; Environmental: Inadequate exposure to sunlight; Gastrointestinal disease: Crohn’s disease]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: A patient with multiple fractures presents with 'Coast of Maine' café-au-lait spots. Identify the underlying syndrome.
back:
- McCune–Albright syndrome.
- Features polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and precocious puberty.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [In patients with precocious puberty and Coast of Maine café-au-lait spots, the diagnosis is McCune–Albright syndrome.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: How does end-stage renal failure contribute to metabolic bone disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism?
back:
- Causes failure of bone mineralisation.
- Triggers compensatory secondary hyperparathyroidism due to renal tubular anomalies.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Table 44.5... Renal disease: End-stage renal failure, renal tubular anomalies. Secondary hyperparathyroidism may be present.]

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
front: Q: What is the typical mechanical threshold for a 'fragility fracture' in an osteoporotic patient?
back: - A fall from standing height.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic bone is liable to fracture with low-energy injuries (e.g. a fall from standing height).]

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: * Failure of structurally abnormal bone under normal physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Differentiate pathological from traumatic fractures based on the force required.
back: * Traumatic: Excessive force applied to normal bone. * Pathological: Minimal or normal force applied to weakened/diseased bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Contrast the healing potential of traumatic versus pathological fractures.
back: * Traumatic: Healthy bone follows standard union timelines. * Pathological: Bone may fail to heal entirely depending on the underlying pathology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal"

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: An elderly patient presents with a femur fracture after sitting down. What is the diagnosis?
back: * Pathological fracture (mechanism inconsistent with injury severity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Why is load-bearing fixation preferred over load-sharing for pathological fractures?
back: * Abnormal bone cannot reliably support weight during union. * The implant must carry the physiological load indefinitely to prevent failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: List four common systemic causes of pathological fractures.
back: * Primary bone tumors. * Metastatic deposits. * Osteomyelitis. * Metabolic bone disease (e.g., Osteoporosis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis)."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Describe the management of an 'impending' pathological fracture identified before failure.
back: * Prophylactic surgical stabilization with a load-bearing device.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: How does the management of periarticular pathological fractures differ from traumatic articular injuries?
back: * Pathological: Often requires en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty. * Traumatic: Usually managed with anatomical reduction and internal fixation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Name three metabolic conditions that weaken bone leading to pathological failure.
back: * Osteomalacia. * Paget’s disease. * Osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis)."

category: Define pathological fractures and differentiate from traumatic fractures
front: Q: Define the role of arthroplasty in pathological fracture treatment.
back: * It bypasses diseased bone and poor blood supply to allow immediate full weight-bearing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "Arthroplasty in suitable patients bypasses the problems of blood supply and weak bone and allows early full weight-bearing and return to function"

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture.
back: A fracture occurring when abnormal bone fails under normal physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the primary clinical indicator of a pathological fracture in a patient's history?
back: A history of low-energy injury that is inconsistent with the severity of the sustained fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
front: Q: List the specific metabolic bone diseases that cause pathological fractures.
back:
• Osteomalacia
• Paget’s disease
• Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
front: Q: A patient with multiple metastatic bone deposits presents with a hip fracture. What is the management priority?
back:
• Identify the primary tumor source.
• Stabilization using a load-bearing device (not load-sharing).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [In patients with metastatic bone disease, the primary source should be sought if multiple metastatic deposits are identified... stabilization with a load-bearing device may be considered.]

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
front: Q: Which haematological malignancies are known to cause pathological fractures?
back:
• Myeloma
• Lymphoma
• Leukaemia

front: Q: What is the defining characteristic of a pathological fracture?
back: The failure of abnormal bone under normal or minimal physiological load, often due to underlying systemic or local disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is a 'load-bearing' device preferred over 'load-sharing' for pathological fractures?
back: Because the underlying pathology frequently inhibits bone healing, requiring the implant to permanently sustain the full mechanical load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast surgical management of isolated vs. multiple metastatic bone lesions.
back: Isolated: Aggressive curative en bloc excision. Multiple: Palliative stabilization using load-bearing devices to facilitate function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered. If an isolated metastasis is identifed... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Management Strategy: What is the priority when managing a fracture suspected to be a primary bone tumor?
back: Diagnostic identification of the cause while planning surgical treatment specifically to prevent the dissemination of malignant disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the primary pharmacological management to reduce fracture frequency in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment, which decreases bone resorption and turnover to improve bone strength and reduce pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What are the criteria for initiating prophylactic fixation in metastatic bone disease?
back: Identification of a metastatic deposit before a fracture occurs, if clinical assessment indicates an impending fracture is likely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How does a periarticular location influence management of a pathological fracture in a patient with good prognosis?
back: Requires en bloc excision of the lesion followed by primary joint arthroplasty to allow early mobilization and function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is good and the deposit periarticular, an en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty may be considered to optimise return to near normal function.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Diagnosis: A child presents with an anterolateral tibial bow and subsequent non-union fracture. Which underlying condition is suspected?
back: Neurofibromatosis, which is associated with congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia in 50% of cases.
