citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia... presents with an anterolateral bow of the tibia with or without a fracture... 50% are associated with neurofbromatosis.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: List the common metabolic bone diseases leading to pathological fractures mentioned in the text.
back:
1. Osteoporosis
2. Osteomalacia
3. Paget’s disease
4. Rickets
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [...metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).] and Page 614 (Book Page): [In rickets... deformity is common.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the primary surgical goal for stabilizing osteoporotic lower limb fractures in the elderly?
back: Fixation must be strong enough to support immediate full weight-bearing and maintain alignment until union occurs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Treatment of lower limb osteoporotic fractures... should be strong enough to allow immediate weight-bearing and to hold the position until union.]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Define a complete fracture regarding cortical involvement.
back: A complete fracture involves failure across the whole bone, extending through the entire circumference of both cortices.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [adult transverse fracture failure across the whole bone]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Describe the mechanical failure mechanism of a greenstick fracture.
back: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture where one tension cortex fails (breaks) while the opposite (compression) cortex remains intact or bent.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [incomplete fractures are called greenstick... fractures, where one tension cortex fails.]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Contrast the cortical appearance of Torus vs. Greenstick fractures.
back:
● Torus (Buckle): Compression cortex buckles outward.
● Greenstick: Tension cortex fails/breaks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Greenstick... fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: A 6-year-old presents with wrist pain. X-ray shows a localized bulge on the distal radius cortex without a clear break line. Diagnosis?
back: Torus (Buckle) fracture; a type of incomplete fracture characteristic of the soft, plastic nature of pediatric bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Why do incomplete fractures occur predominantly in children rather than adults?
back: Pediatric bones are more plastic and less brittle than adult bones, allowing for failure of only one side of the bone under stress.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [In children and adolescents the fracture line may be incomplete because of the plastic, less brittle nature of their bones]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: What defines "plastic deformation" in pediatric bone injury?
back: Bending of the bone under stress without a visible fracture line on radiographs; an extreme form of incomplete injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Paediatric bone may also simply undergo plastic deformation without a visible fracture line.]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: How does the management of extra-articular pediatric fractures utilize their incomplete nature?
back: Reduction often uses the intact periosteal hinge (typical of incomplete fractures) to guide fragments and maintain alignment during casting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [The periosteal hinge should be preserved as it also allows for better holding of the fracture if it remains intact]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Differentiate between the mechanical failure of adult vs. pediatric long bone diaphyses.
back:
● Adult: Failure is typically complete across both cortices.
● Pediatric: Often incomplete (Greenstick/Torus) due to higher elastic/plastic capacity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [(b) adult transverse fracture failure across the whole bone; (c) greenstick fracture; the bone has failed on the tension side]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Describe the structural state of the compression side in a greenstick injury.
back: The compression cortex does not break but remains intact, though it may undergo plastic bending/deformation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [greenstick... fractures, where one tension cortex fails... the remaining mechanical properties are used to achieve stability.]

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
front: Q: Identify the three primary types of incomplete pediatric bone injuries.
back:
1. Greenstick fracture
2. Torus (Buckle) fracture
3. Plastic deformation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Incomplete fractures are called greenstick... torus or buckle fractures... plastic deformation without a visible fracture line.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: When is a fracture clinically defined as "pathological"?
back: A: When abnormal bone fails under a normal load, usually due to underlying disease weakening the skeletal structure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why are load-bearing devices preferred over load-sharing in pathological fractures?
back: A: Pathological bone often fails to heal due to the underlying condition; therefore, the implant must bear the entire physiological load independently.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the management strategy for a pathological fracture involving a joint surface?
back:
A: 
- En bloc excision of the affected area
- Reconstruction via joint replacement (arthroplasty)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Clinical Scenario: A patient has a metastatic deposit with an impending fracture. Correct intervention?
back:
A: 
- Prophylactic stabilization with a load-bearing device
- Prevents complete fracture and optimizes functional return
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How must surgery be modified if the pathological fracture is suspected to be a primary tumor?
back: A: Treatment must be specifically planned to prevent disseminating the disease throughout the tissues during surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What clinical finding is the primary indicator for a suspected pathological fracture?
back: A: A history where the mechanism (e.g., low-energy injury) is inconsistent with the severity of the fracture sustained.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Management: A patient with multiple metastases and poor life expectancy suffers a pathological fracture.
back: A: Palliative stabilization using a load-bearing device to provide pain relief and allow immediate mobility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [In patients with metastatic bone disease... If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast management of a solitary metastasis versus widespread secondary deposits in bone.
back:
A: 
- Solitary: Aggressive curative approach (en bloc excision of primary and secondary).
- Widespread: Stabilization for functional maintenance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is early mobilization critical in treating geriatric pathological fractures?
back: A: Older patients often cannot follow non-weight-bearing restrictions; fixation must be strong enough to allow immediate full weight-bearing to prevent complications.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [As there may be additional and pre-existing mobility problems, such patients are unable to partially weight-bear and so fxation should be strong enough to allow immediate weight-bearing]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: List the four non-malignant metabolic causes of pathological fractures named in the text.
back:
A: 
- Osteomalacia
- Paget’s disease
- Osteoporosis
- Osteomyelitis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What clinical clue most strongly suggests a pathological fracture rather than standard trauma?
back: A history of low-energy injury that is inconsistent with the resulting fracture severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What underlying systemic disease states typically lead to the development of pathological fractures?
back:
• Primary or metastatic bone tumours
• Haematological malignancies (e.g., Myeloma)
• Osteomyelitis
• Metabolic bone disease (Paget’s, Osteoporosis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic diagnostic features of a Brodie’s abscess from an aggressive pathological lesion.
back: Brodie’s abscess presents as a sclerotic-walled cyst, while aggressive pathological fractures show irregular cortical lysis or bone destruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Brodie’s abscess: Chronic infections may present with radiographic features of a sclerotic walled cyst.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: A 70-year-old with back pain shows a compression fracture; which 'red flags' demand malignancy screening?
back:
• Unrelenting or night pain
• Systemic illness/weight loss
• Progressive neurological deficit
• Significant spinal deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): [‘Red fag’ symptoms and signs for spinal pathology: Systemic illness, fever or weight loss; Progressive neurological defcit; Unrelenting or night pain; Spinal deformity.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which specific laboratory investigations are essential for evaluating the etiology of suspected pathological fractures?
back:
• Full blood count (FBC)
• Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
• C-reactive protein (CRP).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): [All ‘red fag’ signs require urgent investigation with a full blood count (FBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), plain radiograph and MRI or other imaging.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which imaging modality is indicated to identify the primary source in suspected metastatic pathological fractures?
back: Whole-body CT or MRI is utilized to identify primary sources and multi-focal metastatic deposits.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [In patients with metastatic bone disease, the primary source should be sought if multiple metastatic deposits are identifed... further imaging such as MRI may be required.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: How does finding an isolated metastasis versus multiple deposits alter the diagnostic and management approach?
back: Isolated metastases with good prognosis may require aggressive curative en bloc excision rather than simple stabilization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: A child presents with an atraumatic femoral neck slip; what metabolic/hormonal conditions must be ruled out?
back:
• Hypothyroidism
• Renal failure
• History of previous local or pituitary radiotherapy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Other conditions such as hypothyroidism, renal failure and previous radiotherapy treatment (local or to the pituitary) also increase the risk (of SCFE).]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is a 'sympathetic joint effusion' a potential diagnostic pitfall in metaphyseal osteomyelitis?
back: Inflammation from adjacent bone infection can cause reactive fluid accumulation in the joint without direct bacterial invasion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [The diferentiation between the two may be difcult and a sympathetic joint efusion may occur with metaphyseal osteomyelitis.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which radiographic feature is pathognomonic for non-accidental injury causing pediatric pathological fractures?
back: Metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Figure 44.43 Anteroposterior radiograph of a knee showing metaphyseal corner fractures that are considered to be pathognomonic of non-accidental injury.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of a pathological fracture?
back: The failure of abnormal bone under normal physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which major disease categories can weaken bone enough to cause a pathological fracture?
back:
• Primary bone tumours
• Secondary metastatic deposits
• Haematological malignancies (e.g., myeloma)
• Metabolic bone disease
• Osteomyelitis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What feature of patient history is the most important indicator of a pathological fracture?
back: A history of a low-energy injury mechanism that is inconsistent with the resulting fracture severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the immediate diagnostic priority when multiple metastatic deposits are identified alongside a fracture?
back: The clinician must actively seek and identify the primary source of the malignancy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [In patients with metastatic bone disease, the primary source should be sought if multiple metastatic deposits are identified.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What diagnostic and management precaution is mandatory if a primary bone tumour is suspected?
back: Treatment and biopsy must be meticulously planned specifically to prevent the dissemination of the disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the diagnostic hallmark of an 'impending' pathological fracture?
back: The identification of a metastatic bone deposit prior to an actual fracture event occurring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identified prior to fracture, prophylactic fixation should be considered if impending fracture is likely.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: How do CT scans assist in the diagnosis of complex pathological fractures?
back: They allow for the appreciation of injury severity and multiplanar characterization of underlying bony anatomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The severity of the injury is often best appreciated with CT scans.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: In cases of chronic infection causing bone failure, what diagnostic findings confirm osteomyelitis?
back:
• Positive culture from deep surgical samples
• Histopathological evidence of infection
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 604 (Book Page): [Confirmation of the diagnosis is with culture from deep surgical samples and histology.]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which metabolic conditions should be screened for in elderly patients with pathological fractures?
back:
• Osteomalacia
• Paget’s disease
• Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What unique radiographic feature may identify a pathological fracture caused by a Brodie’s abscess?
back: The presence of a sclerotic walled cyst in the bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Brodie’s abscess: Chronic infections may present with radiographic features of a sclerotic walled cyst.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which haematological malignancies are major causes of pathological fractures?
back:
• Myeloma
• Lymphoma
• Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)...]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What clinical history should immediately trigger suspicion of a pathological fracture?
back: A history of low-energy injury that is inconsistent with the resulting fracture severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: List the metabolic bone diseases that weaken bone leading to pathological fractures.
back:
• Osteomalacia
• Paget’s disease
• Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [...metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the management for an isolated metastatic deposit with a good curative prognosis?
back: En bloc excision of both the primary tumour and the isolated secondary deposit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is offered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why are load-bearing devices preferred over load-sharing ones for pathological fractures?
back: Abnormal bone involved in pathological fractures often fails to heal reliably; load-bearing devices provide essential definitive stability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: When is prophylactic fixation indicated for a metastatic bone lesion?
back: When a metastatic deposit is identified and an impending fracture is considered likely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How is a periarticular metastatic deposit managed in a patient with good life expectancy?
back:
• En bloc excision of the affected area
• Primary joint arthroplasty
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is good and the deposit periarticular, an en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty may be considered to optimise return to near normal function as soon as possible.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the primary concern when managing a fracture suspected to be a primary bone tumour?
back: Treatment must be planned specifically to prevent the dissemination of the disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease (see Chapter 42).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the goal of management for metastatic pathological fractures with poor life expectancy?
back: Palliative stabilization using a load-bearing device.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Name two non-neoplastic causes of pathological fractures according to the text.
back:
• Osteomyelitis
• Metabolic bone disease
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease...]

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What clinical hallmark differentiates a pathological fracture from a standard traumatic fracture?
back: A history of low-energy injury that is inconsistent with the severity of the resulting bone failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which three hematological malignancies are primary diagnostic considerations in pathological fractures?
back:
* Multiple Myeloma.
* Lymphoma.
* Leukaemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "The bone may be weakened by... haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)"

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast the diagnostic priorities between primary bone tumors and metastatic deposits in fractures.
back:
* Primary: Prevent disease dissemination during diagnostic/surgical planning.
* Metastatic: Actively seek the primary source (e.g., Lung, Breast) if multiple deposits exist.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease. In patients with metastatic bone disease, the primary source should be sought if multiple metastatic deposits are identified."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: An elderly patient suffers a hip fracture after a simple sneeze. What is the immediate diagnostic priority?
back:
* Confirm the fracture is pathological.
* Actively seek an underlying cause (Oncological, Metabolic, or Infective).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury... if a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: List the metabolic bone diseases that cause diagnostic confusion with neoplastic pathological fractures.
back:
* Osteomalacia.
* Paget’s disease.
* Osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis)."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: In maxillofacial trauma, what specifically defines a fracture as "pathological"?
back: The fracture occurs through an existing local lesion, specifically a neoplastic or inflammatory process.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): "pathological (through an existing lesion such as neoplastic or inflammatory)."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the recommended management approach for an identified "impending" pathological fracture?
back: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing (rather than load-sharing) device.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "If a metastatic deposit is identified prior to fracture, prophylactic fixation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: How does the diagnostic approach change for a solitary metastasis versus multiple metastatic deposits?
back:
* Solitary: Consider aggressive curative en bloc excision if prognosis is good.
* Multiple: Seek primary source and prioritize palliative stabilization for survival.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered. If an isolated metastasis is identified... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Explain why load-bearing devices are preferred over load-sharing for pathological fracture stabilization.
back: Abnormal bone involved in pathological fractures may fail to heal, necessitating a device that carries the entire physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing."

category: Describe diagnostic approaches for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which infectious condition must be ruled out during the workup of a non-traumatic pathological fracture?
back: Osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): "The bone may be weakened by... osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease... When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture."

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the preferred management option for pathological fractures involving the joint surface?
back: The affected area should be excised en bloc and a joint replacement (arthroplasty) performed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the affected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is a load-bearing device specifically chosen for pathological fracture fixation?
back: Abnormal bone may fail to heal; load-bearing devices support physiological stress independently of bone union.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast the management of pathological fractures in patients with poor versus good life expectancy.
back:
• Poor expectancy: Simple stabilization with load-bearing devices.
• Good expectancy: Aggressive curative en bloc excision and reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered. If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Clinical Scenario: A patient presents with a single metastatic humeral fracture and a curative oncology prognosis. Plan management.
back: Perform an aggressive curative approach involving en bloc excision of the primary tumor and the isolated secondary deposit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the advocated surgical step for an identified metastatic deposit with an impending fracture?
back: Prophylactic fixation using a load-bearing stabilization device.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered... load-bearing device is once again advocated.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which clinical observation must trigger an active search for an underlying cause of fracture?
back: A history of low-energy injury that is inconsistent with the severity of the resulting fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture. If a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How is the concept of 'load-sharing' versus 'load-bearing' applied to pathological bone management?
back: Load-sharing (e.g., standard screws) is avoided because it relies on bone healing, which is frequently absent in pathological failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Case: A primary bone tumor is the suspected cause of an acute fracture. What is the priority?
back: Plan treatment specifically to prevent disseminating the disease while addressing the fracture stabilization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which hematological malignancies commonly cause bone weakening requiring surgical stabilization?
back:
• Myeloma
• Lymphoma
• Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: List the metabolic bone diseases that serve as underlying causes for pathological fractures.
back:
• Osteomalacia
• Paget’s disease
• Osteoporosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by] metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Define a pathological fracture according to skeletal failure mechanics.
back: A fracture occurring when abnormal bone fails under a normal, physiological load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why are load-bearing implants preferred over load-sharing devices for pathological fractures?
back: The underlying abnormal bone may not heal; a load-bearing device is required to sustain permanent weight independently of bone support.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which historical detail is the primary hallmark for suspecting a pathological fracture?
back: A history of a low-energy injury mechanism that is inconsistent with the resulting fracture severity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How is management altered when a primary bone tumor is the suspected cause of a fracture?
back: Treatment must be specifically planned to prevent the dissemination of the disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which drug class is used to reduce pain and pathological fracture rates in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Cyclical bisphosphonates, which decrease bone resorption and turnover.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate...]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: List three haematological malignancies frequently associated with pathological fractures.
back:
1. Myeloma
2. Lymphoma
3. Leukaemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)...]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the recommended strategy for an isolated metastasis with a good prognosis?
back: An aggressive curative approach involving en bloc excision of the primary tumor and the isolated secondary deposit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identified and an overall good prognosis is offered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision...]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast the management of periarticular versus shaft metastatic deposits in patients with long life expectancy.
back: Shaft lesions require load-bearing stabilization; periarticular lesions may require en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty for functional optimization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is good and the deposit periarticular, an en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty may be considered to optimise return to near normal function as soon as possible.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How do metabolic conditions like Paget’s disease or osteomalacia contribute to fracture risk?
back: They weaken the internal bone structure, allowing failure under normal, everyday loads.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget's disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the indicated management for a metastatic deposit that hasn't yet fractured?
back: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing device if a fracture is deemed impending.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identified prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What defines the mechanism of a pathological fracture in musculoskeletal medicine?
back: A: Failure of abnormal bone under normal physiological load, often due to underlying weakening from disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why are load-bearing implants mandatory over load-sharing devices for pathological fracture management?
back: A: The underlying pathology often prevents reliable bone union, requiring the implant to sustain weight indefinitely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Differentiate the surgical management of periarticular versus diaphyseal pathological fractures.
back:
A: * Diaphyseal: Internal stabilization (e.g., IM nail).
* Periarticular: En bloc excision followed by joint arthroplasty.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: A patient with isolated bone metastasis has a curative prognosis; what is the indicated management?
back: A: Aggressive en bloc excision of both the primary tumor and the secondary deposit for curative intent.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What pharmacological intervention is used to reduce fracture risk in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: A: Cyclical bisphosphonates; these decrease bone resorption and turnover to enhance mineral density.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: List three primary diagnostic categories that cause pathological bone weakening.
back:
A: 1. Metastatic deposits.
2. Metabolic disease (e.g., Paget’s, Osteomalacia).
3. Haematological malignancy (e.g., Myeloma).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and meta - bolic bone disease.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How does life expectancy dictate stabilization choices in metastatic bone disease?
back:
A: * Poor expectancy: Palliative stabilization via load-bearing implants.
* Good expectancy: Radical en bloc excision and reconstructive surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered. If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered... a more aggressive curative approach may be taken.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: When is prophylactic internal fixation indicated for a non-fractured bone lesion?
back: A: When radiographic assessment or clinical symptoms identify an impending fracture likely to occur with weight-bearing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, pro - phylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is intramedullary stabilization preferred over plates in osteogenesis imperfecta fractures?
back: A: Nails maintain alignment while allowing for bone growth and providing internal splintage against further deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Intramedullary techniques for stabilisation of fractures or osteotomies are preferred to plate fxation. Rehabilitation should start promptly.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What clinical finding should raise suspicion of a pathological fracture over a traumatic one?
back: A: A mechanism of injury inconsistent with fracture severity (e.g., low-energy trauma causing high-grade failure).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How is a pathological fracture defined in MSK medicine?
back: A fracture that occurs when abnormal bone fails under a level of mechanical load that would be considered normal for healthy bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [When abnormal bone fails under normal load this is referred to as a pathological fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is a load-bearing device preferred over load-sharing for pathological fractures?
back: Because abnormal or diseased bone may not heal reliably; the implant must therefore be capable of carrying the entire physiological load independently.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast the surgical management of pathological fractures in patients with poor versus good life expectancy.
back:
● Poor: Palliative stabilization with a load-bearing device.
● Good: Aggressive curative approach involving en bloc excision of the primary and secondary deposits.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered. If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: A patient is found to have an isolated metastatic lesion before a fracture occurs. What is the recommended management?
back: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing device to prevent an impending fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What precaution must be taken when managing a pathological fracture suspected to be a primary bone tumor?
back: Treatment must be specifically planned to avoid spreading or disseminating the disease during the surgical procedure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease (see Chapter 42 ).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What clinical finding regarding the injury mechanism is highly suspicious for a pathological fracture?
back: A fracture resulting from low-energy trauma or a mechanism inconsistent with the severity of the bone injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [A pathological fracture should be suspected if the history is not consistent with the severity of the injury. The patient may give a history of low-energy injury that normally would not cause a fracture.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: When is joint arthroplasty indicated as a management option for a pathological fracture?
back: When the fracture involves the joint surface or is periarticular, combined with a good patient life expectancy to optimize functional return.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed. ... If life expectancy is good and the deposit periarticular, an en bloc excision and joint arthroplasty may be considered to optimise return to near normal function as soon as possible.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
coreConcept: Systemic Etiology of Pathological Bone Failure
front: Q: List the four broad categories of systemic disease that cause pathological fractures.
back:
1. Metastatic deposits/Primary tumors.
2. Hematological malignancies (Myeloma/Leukaemia).
3. Infection (Osteomyelitis).
4. Metabolic disease (Osteomalacia/Paget’s/Osteoporosis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Name the two metabolic bone diseases (excluding osteoporosis) that commonly weaken bone enough to cause fractures.
back:
● Osteomalacia.
● Paget’s disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which specific hematological malignancies are associated with a high risk of pathological fractures?
back:
● Myeloma.
● Lymphoma.
● Leukaemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Which ligament is most frequently injured in lateral ankle sprains?
back: The Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL). It spans from the distal fibula to the lateral talus to prevent inversion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): The ATFL is the most frequently injured ligament in the complex; it attaches at the most distal aspect of the fbula and spans anteromedially to the lateral aspect of the talus to prevent inversion during plantarfexion.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Describe the classic non-contact mechanism of an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) injury.
back: A sudden deceleration where the knee falls into valgus while the tibia externally rotates, causing a knee subluxation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): The most common mechanism of these injuries is a deceleration when the knee falls into valgus and the tibia externally rotates, leading to a subluxation of the knee.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Differentiate the diagnostic maneuvers for Tennis elbow versus Golfer's elbow.
back:
• Tennis Elbow (Lateral): Pain during resisted wrist extension.
• Golfer's Elbow (Medial): Pain during resisted wrist flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 485 (Book Page): Resisted wrist fexion, which reproduces the pain over the medial epicondyle (Golfer's)... Wrist extension against resistance with the elbow extended should provoke the patient’s symptoms (Tennis).

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: An athlete presents with tense proptosis and reduced visual acuity after facial trauma. Immediate management?
back: Emergency bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis to relieve pressure on the retinal artery and optic nerve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity... If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Identify the 'gold standard' surgical reconstruction for a chronic Ulnar Collateral Ligament (UCL) tear.
back: 'Tommy John' surgery (UCL reconstruction) using a harvested autograft tendon, typically the palmaris longus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): the gold standard for surgical treatment is UCL reconstruction or Tommy John surgery. The surgery involves an autograft tendon harvest, commonly utilising the ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: List the three main Ottawa rules for indicated ankle radiographs.
back:
1. Bone tenderness at the posterior margin/tip of lateral malleolus.
2. Bone tenderness at the posterior margin/tip of medial malleolus.
3. Inability to bear weight immediately and during exam.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): TABLE 36.1 Ottawa ankle rules. ● Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus ● Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the medial malleolus ● Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Explain the clinical significance of a Segond fracture in a sports injury context.
back: A Segond fracture (anterolateral tibial avulsion) is pathognomonic for an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Define the clinical presentation and cause of Osgood–Schlatter disease.
back: Traction apophysitis of the patellar tendon at the tibial tubercle. Presents as pain and swelling exacerbated by exercise in adolescents.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): Osgood–Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the patellar tendon insertion. Pain, tenderness and swelling at the tibial tubercle, exacerbated by exercise, are diagnostic.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Describe the 'milking manoeuvre' for diagnosing Ulnar Collateral Ligament (UCL) injuries.
back: The examiner pulls the patient's thumb with downward force while stabilizing the flexed elbow to elicit medial pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): milking manoeuvre (Figure 36.3), in which the examiner provides a valgus stress through elbow range of motion. Pain at the medial elbow during these manoeuvres is specifc for UCL pathology.

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: What is the 'C-sign' and which two hip pathologies does it typically indicate?
back: Patient places hand in a 'C' shape over the anterolateral groin. Indicates Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) or Hip Dysplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 503 (Book Page): Intra-articular hip derangements most commonly manifest as anterolateral groin pain in a characteristic distribution, referred to as a ‘C-sign’ (Figure 36.4). In a young patient, two common sources... are femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and dysplasia.

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the initial management step when a pathological fracture is clinically suspected?
back:
- Actively investigate the underlying etiology (primary/metastatic tumor, metabolic disease, or infection).
- Identify the primary source in metastatic cases.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a pathological fracture is suspected, the cause should be actively sought. In patients with metastatic bone disease, the primary source should be sought if multiple metastatic deposits are identifed.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is load-bearing fixation preferred over load-sharing in pathological fractures?
back:
- Pathologically abnormal bone has extremely poor healing potential.
- Load-bearing devices provide stability independent of biological bone union.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What management is indicated for pathological fractures involving joint surfaces?
back:
- En bloc excision of the affected bone segment.
- Reconstruction using primary joint arthroplasty.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How should a pathological fracture be managed in a patient with multiple metastases and poor life expectancy?
back:
- Palliative stabilization of the limb.
- Implementation of a load-bearing fixation device.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the surgical strategy for an isolated metastatic pathological fracture with a good prognosis?
back:
- Aggressive curative approach.
- Concurrent en bloc excision of the primary source and the secondary deposit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which underlying disease categories are high-yield causes of pathological bone failure?
back:
- Bone tumors (Primary/Metastatic).
- Hematological malignancies (Myeloma/Leukaemia).
- Metabolic bone disease (Osteomalacia/Paget's).
- Osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by a primary bone tumour, secondary metastatic deposits, haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia), osteomyelitis and metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Describe the management of a metastatic bone deposit with an impending fracture.
back:
- Prophylactic surgical stabilization.
- Preference for load-bearing fixation to prevent displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, pro - phylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What precaution must be observed when managing a fracture suspected to be a primary bone tumor?
back: - Specific surgical planning to prevent local or systemic dissemination of neoplastic cells.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why is non-union a critical consideration in the mechanical loop of pathological fracture management?
back:
- Abnormal bone frequently fails to reach union.
- Implants must survive indefinitely without the biological support of healed bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Name three specific hematological malignancies that cause pathological bone weakening.
back:
- Multiple Myeloma.
- Lymphoma.
- Leukaemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [The bone may be weakened by ... haematological malignancy (myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia)]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the mandatory mechanical characteristic of implants used for pathological fractures?
back: The use of load-bearing rather than load-sharing devices is required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Why are load-bearing implants preferred over load-sharing ones in pathological fractures?
back: Abnormal bone often fails to heal reliably, meaning the implant must permanently support the full load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Depending on the cause of the pathological fracture the bone may not heal and consideration should be given to a load-bearing device not load-sharing.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Contrast the surgical management of a solitary bone metastasis versus multiple deposits.
back:
● Solitary: Aggressive en bloc excision of primary and secondary lesions.
● Multiple: Stabilization with load-bearing devices or palliation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If an isolated metastasis is identifed and an overall good prognosis is ofered by the oncologists, a more aggressive curative approach may be taken with en bloc excision of the primary and the isolated secondary deposit. If life expectancy is poor, then stabilisation with a load-bearing device may be considered.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the preferred management for a pathological fracture involving the joint surface?
back: En bloc excision of the affected area followed by joint replacement (arthroplasty).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: How are structural bone voids managed during the fixation of pathological fractures?
back: Utilize injectable bone substitutes or bone cement to fill voids and augment fixation strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 432 (Book Page): [Injectable bone substitutes may be used to fll bone voids and augment fxation.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: When is joint arthroplasty indicated as the primary treatment for a pathological injury?
back:
● Fracture involves/near the joint surface.
● Reconstruction is technically impossible.
● Weak bone makes fixation unreliable.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed. ... Arthroplasty in suitable patients bypasses the problems of blood supply and weak bone]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: What is the critical precaution when managing a fracture caused by a suspected primary bone tumor?
back: Treatment must be carefully planned specifically to prevent the dissemination of the disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Where a primary bone tumour is suspected, treatment should be planned to prevent disseminating the disease.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Describe the management of an identified bone metastasis before it actually fractures.
back: Prophylactic stabilization using a load-bearing device to prevent impending fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [If a metastatic deposit is identifed prior to fracture, prophylactic fxation should be considered if impending fracture is likely. Prophylactic stabilisation with a load-bearing device is once again advocated.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
coreConcept: Locking plate mechanics in weak bone
front: Q: Why is locking plate technology specifically used for elderly patients with pathological fragility?
back: The screw threads into the plate, preventing it from cutting out of soft metaphyseal bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 431 (Book Page)-432: [Locking plate technology improves fxation in osteoporotic bone... where the screw secures itself into the plate... may help reduce failure of fxation in osteoporotic bone.]

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
front: Q: Which two factors determine if a periprosthetic fracture requires primary replacement (revision)?
back:
● Existing implant is loose.
● Insufficient bone stock remains to support fixation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 437 (Book Page): [surgical decision making is infuenced by whether the implant is attached to bone or is loose, the amount of bone to fx into... primary and revision arthroplasty have been considered in these situations]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Which specific arm positions typically precipitate an acute anterior shoulder dislocation in athletes?
back: Forced abduction and external rotation of the shoulder.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 500 (Book Page): '...anterior shoulder dislocations can occur in instances of traumatic or forced shoulder abduction and external rotation.'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: In repetitive throwing athletes, which specific phase of the throwing cycle places maximum stress on the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL)?
back: The late cocking and early acceleration phases.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): 'In the late cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing the ligament is under its maximum stress and at this stage is at the highest risk of rupture and chronic attenuation.'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Describe the 'C-sign' used by young patients to describe intra-articular hip derangements.
back: A hand gesture indicating anterolateral groin pain, typically signaling femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) or dysplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 503 (Book Page): 'Intra-articular hip derangements most commonly manifest as anterolateral groin pain in a characteristic distribution, referred to as a “C-sign” (Figure 36.4).'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: A football player feels a 'pop' and presents with immediate hemarthrosis and a positive Lachman test. Identify the pathognomonic fracture for this ligamentous injury.
back: Segond fracture (located on the anterolateral tibia), diagnostic of an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): 'A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: What is the 'gold standard' surgical management for high-level pitchers with complete UCL rupture?
back: UCL reconstruction (Tommy John surgery), typically utilizing an ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon autograft.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): '...the gold standard for surgical treatment is UCL reconstruction or Tommy John surgery. The surgery involves an autograft tendon harvest, commonly utilising the ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon...'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: List the three Ottawa ankle rules determining the requirement for radiography after a sprain.
back:
1. Bone tenderness at posterior margin/tip of lateral malleolus.
2. Bone tenderness at posterior margin/tip of medial malleolus.
3. Inability to bear weight immediately and at examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): 'Table 36.1 Ottawa ankle rules. ● Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus ● Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the medial malleolus ● Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Describe 'intersection syndrome' often seen in competitive rowers.
back: A tendinosis occurring where the first and second extensor tendon compartments of the forearm cross, caused by repetitive motion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 506 (Book Page): 'Forearm tendon issues such as intersection syndrome (a tendinosis where the frst and second extensor tendon compartments of the forearm cross) are also a commonly encountered problem in rowing athletes.'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: A pediatric patient presents with a 'white eye' blow-out orbital fracture. Which triad constitutes the resulting emergency reflex?
back: The oculocardiac reflex: bradycardia, nausea, and syncope (indicating inferior rectus muscle entrapment).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page)/413: 'Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Identify the three metabolic and physiological components of the 'Female Athlete Triad'.
back:
1. Osteoporosis.
2. Disordered eating.
3. Amenorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 507 (Book Page): 'Stress fractures... can be more frequent in the female athlete triad (osteoporosis, disordered eating and amenorrhoea).'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Which lateral ankle ligament is most frequently injured during an inversion sprain?
back: Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): 'The ATFL is the most frequently injured ligament in the complex; it attaches at the most distal aspect of the fbula and spans anteromedially to the lateral aspect of the talus to prevent inversion during plantarfexion.'

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: What are the three specific ligaments of the lateral collateral complex involved in a low ankle sprain?
back:
1. Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) - most common.
2. Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL).
3. Posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): [The ankle primarily resists inversion through the lateral collateral ligament complex, which is composed of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL).]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Describe the gold standard surgical management for a chronic ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) tear in throwing athletes.
back: Tommy John Surgery: Autograft tendon reconstruction (usually palmaris longus) through bone tunnels drilled into the humerus and ulna.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): [the gold standard for surgical treatment is UCL reconstruction or Tommy John surgery. The surgery involves an autograft tendon harvest, commonly utilising the ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon, and reconstruction of the ligament through bone tunnels in both the humerus and ulna.]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Identify two pathognomonic radiological signs of an acute Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) injury.
back:
1. Segond fracture (avulsion of the anterolateral tibia).
2. "Kissing lesions" (bone marrow edema on posterolateral tibia and lateral femoral condyle on MRI).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury... ‘Kissing lesions’ of bony oedema seen on fluid-sensitive sequences on the posterolateral tibia and lateral femoral condyle are also pathognomonic for ACL rupture]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: A baseball pitcher presents with medial elbow pain reproduced by valgus stress through elbow range of motion. What is the diagnosis?
back: Ulnar Collateral Ligament (UCL) tear (identified via the Milking Manoeuvre or Moving Valgus Stress Test).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): [milking manoeuvre ( Figure 36.3 ), in which the examiner provides a valgus stress through elbow range of motion. Pain at the medial elbow during these manoeuvres is specific for UCL pathology.]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: What is the immediate surgical management for a sports-related retrobulbar hemorrhage presenting with proptosis and loss of pupillary response?
back: Bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis to decompress the orbit and prevent retinal artery ischemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Retrobulbar haemorrhage... presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response... preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: List the clinical criteria of the Ottawa Ankle Rules that necessitate radiographs in acute trauma.
back:
1. Bone tenderness at posterior margin/tip of lateral malleolus.
2. Bone tenderness at posterior margin/tip of medial malleolus.
3. Inability to bear weight immediately and at examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): [Table 36.1 Ottawa ankle rules... Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus... medial malleolus... Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Contrast the common secondary pathologies of anterior shoulder dislocation in young vs. older athletes.
back: Young (<30 years): Anteroinferior labral tears and high risk of recurrent instability. Older: Acute rotator cuff tears.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 501 (Book Page): [In athletes younger than 30 years old... tearing of the anteroinferior labrum... In older patients who experience falls and sustain the same anterior shoulder dislocations, additional pathologies, including rotator cuff tears, can occur.]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
front: Q: Differentiate "Tennis Elbow" from "Golfer’s Elbow" by their respective anatomical origins.
back: Tennis Elbow: Lateral epicondylitis (extensor carpi radialis brevis origin). Golfer’s Elbow: Medial epicondylitis (fexor pronator mass origin).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 485 (Book Page): [Medial epicondylitis (synonym golfer’s elbow). The medial epicondyle is the common origin of the forearm flexors... Lateral epicondylitis (synonym tennis elbow). The lateral epicondyle is the common origin of the forearm extensors.]

category: Classify sports injuries and their management
